extracted.intended_audience: media studies students, researchers, and scholars; journalists and policy analysts interested in patterns of media content and content analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and patterns for analyzing media content (news and entertainment), including measures of balance, violence, deviance, source and topic selection, geographic and demographic representation, and framing. Draws on empirical studies to identify what makes content newsworthy and how coverage deviates from real-world distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative balance as a standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of measuring balance by quantitative measures (e.g., seconds or amount of airtime given to different institutions or parties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative balance may be misleading because events do not occur in balanced amounts; e.g., Cook (1989) found the U.S. Senate gets more news coverage than the House. Selection of what is covered can bestow importance as much as reflect it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and representativeness of sampled events
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the sample of events/events covered is representative of the domain being described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters cover very few events and then winnow further; 'The sample is by no means representative,' so selection practices can distort perceived importance (Cook, 1989). Evaluate selection bias and the editorial process that confers importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced candidate coverage metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific measures for assessing balance in electoral coverage: number of stories, average length of stories, who initiated subjects, proportion of soundbites used, percent of reinforcing remarks by reporters, objects of visuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in studies of the 1984 presidential election showing ABC/CBS/NBC produced balanced measures across these dimensions (Semetko et al., 1991). When evaluating balance, consider multiple quantitative and qualitative indicators, not just story counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence incidence and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of violent content defined as 'overt expression of physical force' and quantified by percent of shows containing violence, violent acts per hour, and percent of lead characters involved in violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gerbner et al. report high and fairly constant rates (e.g., 70% of prime-time shows, 5.7 violent acts/hour, 54% lead characters involved). Be cautious when comparing television violence rates to real-life crime statistics—the definitions and denominators differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for children's exposure to violent content
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative criterion about who should be held responsible for children's viewing of televised violence (parents vs networks/industry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Network/industry position (e.g., Jack Valenti) emphasizes parental responsibility; critics (e.g., Gerbner) reject 'passing the buck.' Consider policy responses, programming time-slot shifts (MTV moved 'Beavis and Butt-head'), and industry self-regulation or legislative pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of televised violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of program forms contributing to violence on screens: fictional programming, music videos, reality shows, commercials for violent movies, news broadcasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical breakdowns show fictional programming may account for the majority of violent scenes (e.g., 95% of total in one study). Evaluate which formats drive exposure and how promotional material (trailers, commercials) contributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: News preference for violent crime and deaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency of news media to prefer coverage of crimes against people and violent crimes over property or nonviolent crimes, and to report violent deaths more than disease-related deaths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple studies (Ammons et al.; Windhauser et al.; Combs & Slovic) confirm this pattern. When assessing news content, compare the proportion of crime coverage types to real-world incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overreporting of certain crimes (deviance reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: News reporting does not correspond to the relative frequency of crimes; serious offenses (murder, fraud, blackmail, drugs) are often overreported compared to their community occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roshier (1981) found overreporting patterns consistent across papers and time; evaluate whether coverage inflates public perception of risk or punishment probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual content frequency and portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement of sexual acts in programming (e.g., occurrences per hour) and the nature of portrayed sexual behavior (e.g., intercourse primarily between unmarried people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show sexual acts occur with some frequency in prime time and often diverge from real-life patterns; use content counts and contextual coding (relationship status, realism) when evaluating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance as determinant of newsworthiness (statistical and normative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deviance—statistical unusualness or normative rule-breaking—makes events more newsworthy; statistically deviant or norm-breaking events are more likely to be covered and receive prominent placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish statistical deviance (rarity) from normative deviance (law/norm violation). Examples: unusual medical procedures were once newsworthy but became less so as they became common; rape stories require unusual features to be newsworthy now. Evaluate how deviance is operationalized in coverage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and treatment of deviant groups
rubrics_metrics.description: How media portray deviant groups—overreporting severity, focusing on spectacle, sanitizing or downplaying behaviors, emphasizing appearance over message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: British press exaggerating violence (Cohen); accusations of 'sanitizing' gay rights march coverage. Assess tone, focus (appearance vs message), and whether official viewpoints dominate framing (Hertog & McLeod).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping and distortion of mental illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Media tendency to portray the mentally ill as bizarre, dangerous, and outside the mainstream, deviating from expert opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content analyses (Nunnaly, Fruth & Padderred) find emphasis on bizarre symptoms and associating mental illness with criminality. Evaluate frequency, accuracy relative to expert descriptions, and context (daytime serials vs primetime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political deviance framing and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of political nonmainstream actors with condescension, focus on appearance, criminality framing, greater attention to bystanders and official voices than to the protesters' message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hertog & McLeod's study shows local media emphasized appearance and criminality and visually positioned cameras behind police lines. Assess voice balance, visual framing, and privileging of official perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness: conflict and emotional 'sizzle'
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict, salacious detail, and emotional elements ('sizzle') make events more newsworthy and likely to be covered prominently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auletta and others note the press defines newsworthiness by conflict. Topics with emotional resonance (e.g., global warming) get more coverage than less emotional but equally important issues (e.g., sludge). When evaluating topics, measure presence of conflict and emotional hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance of official and 'known' sources
rubrics_metrics.description: News is dominated by 'known' people—incumbent officials, leading federal officials, candidates, and alleged violators—and by official sources from government and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gans (1979) and Sigal (1973) document that prominent and official sources account for a large share of sources. Measure source diversity and the proportion of stories relying on elite/official voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine, source-controlled channels as news origins
rubrics_metrics.description: A large proportion of stories originate through routine, source-controlled channels: official proceedings, press conferences, press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sigal identified almost 60% of stories arising from these channels. Evaluations should code story origins and assess dependence on prepackaged or official materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic selection bias toward official and deviant activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The major activities in news focus on official actions (government conflicts, decisions, ceremonies) and deviant events (protests, crimes, scandals, disasters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gans' typology of prioritized activities can be used to classify coverage; assess whether coverage consistently privileges these topics over others of social significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic coverage bias (coast and beltway biases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneven domestic geographic distribution of news: Pacific Coast and Northeast are overcovered, the Midwest is undercovered; Washington, D.C. stories dominate political coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graber (1988) and others show state coverage is sparse and skewed (e.g., CA and NY received a disproportionate share). Evaluate coverage relative to population or political importance and look for 'beltway bias' in national outlets (e.g., NPR findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: International coverage bias and crisis orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: International news tends to underreport the Third World except during crises, overreport developed countries, focus on events relevant to American interests, and contain more value judgments than domestic coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larson, Wilhoit & Weaver, and Gans document crisis orientation (wars, coups, disasters) and US-centeredness (U.S. referred to in 60% of international stories). Evaluate country selection, topical emphasis (crisis vs routine), and the U.S.-centric framing of foreign news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of 24-hour cable/news networks in international coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Cable networks like CNN can increase the speed of international reporting and provide airplay for voices previously unlikely to reach U.S. audiences, especially during crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNN's simultaneous global broadcasts can empower smaller actors and accelerate multipolar discourse. Assess presence, timeliness, and diversity of foreign voices provided by continuous news channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parachute journalism and loss of specialized foreign correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction in number of foreign correspondents leads to 'parachute journalism'—rapid deployments to hotspots without sustained local expertise—affecting quality of foreign reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate depth, continuity, and reliance on local vs transient reporting; consider how reduced correspondent presence shapes framing and context (FitzSimon, Hess).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational and class representation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Television overrepresents professionals and upper-middle-class occupations and underrepresents clerical, service, middle- and lower-class occupations relative to population distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greenberg, DeFleur, Dominick and others document stable overrepresentation of professionals; compare occupational distributions in media to census data when assessing representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic and racial representation and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Minorities (African Americans, Hispanics, Asians) are often underrepresented and stereotyped in entertainment and news; portrayals often overemphasize crime/victim status or simplified cultural traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: African Americans concentrated in certain program types, more often in minor roles or stereotyped; Hispanics underrepresented in speaking roles. Evaluate frequency, role prestige, stereotypes, and whether coverage privileges white sources/voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender representation and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are underrepresented numerically, depicted younger, concentrated in traditional and subordinate roles (e.g., nurses, secretaries), and stereotyped in magazines and commercials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show ratios favoring men (e.g., two men for every woman historically), age imbalances, and role stereotyping; measure gender counts, role types, relative authority, and presence of gender qualifiers in reporting (e.g., 'female candidate').

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of power relations across demographic axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Media portrayals typically show white males as most authoritative and least likely to be victimized, while minorities, women, the young/old, and lower-class characters are more likely to be victims or stereotyped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gerbner and colleagues link symbolic violence to power—who can get away with aggression—and empirical findings show differential victimizer/victim patterns. When evaluating representation, consider intersectional patterns (race, gender, class, age) and power implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction effects of gender and class in portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship between gender portrayal and social class can invert: working-class TV families show weaker fathers and competent mothers, whereas middle-class families show competent fathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Butsch (1992) documents an inverted relationship; evaluations should account for combined effects of class and gender rather than treating them independently.
